title: Your Short Video Is Losing Before the Point: Write the First Three Seconds First
markdown:
# Your Short Video Is Losing Before the Point: Write the First Three Seconds First

At 9:14 p.m., you post a short video you spent most of the evening making. The edit is clean. The advice is useful. The first comment is a polite “great tips.” The watch graph tells the less polite story: people leave before you get to the thing you made the video for.

That is usually not an editing problem. It is a first-three-seconds problem.

Short-form viewers do not arrive ready to be persuaded. They arrive mid-scroll, with a thumb already moving. Your opening has one job: make stopping feel more sensible than swiping. It does not need to explain the whole video. It needs to create a small, specific tension that the next few seconds resolve.

## The opening is a promise, not an introduction

“Hey everyone, today I’m going to share three tips…” is clear, but it asks for patience before it gives a reason. A stronger opening starts with the cost, the surprise, or the visible result.

Compare these:

> “Today I’m talking about why my meal-prep videos did not perform.”

> “I spent two hours making this meal-prep video. Most viewers left before the pan hit the stove.”

The second version gives the viewer a situation and an unanswered question. What went wrong? Was it the food, the edit, the opening? That gap buys you a few more seconds.

The promise must match the video. A dramatic line that turns into a generic list may win a pause and lose trust. The best hook is not the loudest sentence. It is the most honest sentence that makes the right viewer want the next beat.

## Find the moment where the viewer recognizes themselves

Good hooks often point at a familiar mistake without scolding the person making it. A creator who teaches fitness could begin with, “If your squat feels strong but your knees ache the next day, check this before adding weight.” A designer could say, “Your portfolio may be losing clients at the first screenshot.”

Both lines do three useful things. They name one person, one uncomfortable symptom, and one next step. They also filter. Someone who does not have that problem can scroll on; someone who does has a reason to stay.

Try writing the hook as a sentence that completes this thought:

> “Stop here if you are the person who ______ and keeps getting ______.”

Then remove the throat-clearing. “I want to talk about” almost never survives this edit. Neither does a biography, a channel greeting, or a promise to “get into it.”

## Give the eye something to verify

Words alone can make a claim. A visible detail makes the claim harder to ignore.

If you are showing a repair, begin with the broken part. If you are explaining a workflow, put the messy result on screen before the clean one. If your point is that a tiny change matters, show both versions immediately. The viewer should be able to understand the question with the sound off.

That does not mean cutting every half-second until the video feels frantic. It means putting the evidence near the claim. A close-up, an on-screen number, or a before-and-after frame can carry more weight than another sentence of setup.

## Write several openings for the same video

The first hook that comes to mind is often the one you have heard a hundred times. Give yourself alternatives before you record.

For a video about a photographer whose reels feel flat, you might try:

> “Your photos can be beautiful and still make people swipe.”

> “This is the frame that made my last reel feel expensive instead of slow.”

> “I stopped opening photography reels with the finished shot. Here is why.”

> “If your reel starts with this, the viewer has already decided what happens next.”

Read them out loud. The right one has a natural rhythm, makes a concrete promise, and gives you footage that can appear in the first beat. If the hook needs a paragraph of explanation before it makes sense, it belongs later in the video.

## Match the hook to the payoff

There are a few honest ways to open, and each calls for a different kind of payoff.

- A warning needs a fix or a clear diagnosis soon after it appears.
- A result needs proof that the result is real.
- A question needs a satisfying answer, not a vague lesson.
- A contrarian claim needs the assumption behind it, then the exception.

This is where many openings fail. The creator writes a sharp first line, then follows it with a slow introduction because that is how the script was outlined. Reverse the order. Put the first useful piece directly after the hook. Context can arrive once the viewer has seen why it matters.

## A quick test before you post

Watch the first three seconds with the sound off. Can you tell what the video is about or what problem it will solve? Then listen without looking. Does the first spoken line make sense before the second line explains it?

Finally, ask a tougher question: would someone who does not know you pause for this? Your regular viewers may give you grace. A stranger in a fast feed will not. That is not harsh; it is useful. It tells you where the script has to earn attention.

When an opening almost works, change one thing at a time: the first sentence, the first shot, or the order of the first two beats. Keep the payoff intact. Over a few posts, you will learn which promises your audience actually follows.

## A tool for the blank-page part

Writing five credible versions of one opening takes less time than repairing a weak video after it has been filmed, but it can still be the part that stalls a draft. Hook Lab is built for that moment: give it the video’s subject and the viewer problem, then use the options as raw material. Keep the one that sounds like you and that your video can genuinely deliver.

The goal is not to trick a viewer into watching. It is to put the useful part where a scrolling person can see it in time. Start there, and the rest of the video finally gets a fair chance.
